sections.title: Advanced Strategy for Level 3 Data Sufficiency
sections.content: At this level, questions require analysis in 4–6 steps. It is not only about calculation but also logical testing, checking edge cases (0, negative numbers, fractions, non-integers), and identifying hidden conditions. The answer may be YES or NO, and even if a definite NO is obtained, the data is considered sufficient.

sections.title: Deep Number System Logic
sections.content: Questions based on factors, remainders, prime numbers, and co-primes require careful attention to integer conditions. If n is an integer and n/6 is also an integer, then n must be a multiple of 6. In remainder problems, check whether the divisor is fixed. Also test values like 0 and negative numbers, as they can sometimes produce different outcomes.

sections.title: Zero and Negative Trap
sections.content: If a statement says xy > 0, both numbers could be positive or both negative. If x² = 9, then x = ±3. If there is no condition stating x ≠ 0, then 0 should also be considered a possible value. In Data Sufficiency, do not conclude until all possible values are tested.

sections.title: Abstract Inequalities and Absolute Value
sections.content: Example: Is |x − y| > |x| − |y|? This is not always true. For absolute values, check three cases: both positive, both negative, and one positive while the other negative. If the result changes in any case, the information is insufficient.

sections.title: High-Level Probability
sections.content: If a bag contains red and blue balls and conditional probability is given, the total number of balls and their ratio are required. If only P(Red) is given but the total number is not provided, the exact count cannot be determined. Check whether the information leads to one unique integer solution.

sections.title: Combinatorics Logic
sections.content: Permutation and combination questions involve formulas like nCr or nPr. If only the value of a combination is given but n is not clearly defined, multiple solutions may exist. Check whether only one value is possible or several.

sections.title: A Definitive NO Is Also Sufficient
sections.content: If the question asks: 'Is x prime?' and the statement proves that x is an even number greater than 2, then the definite answer is NO. This is also sufficient data because the answer is certain.

sections.title: 4–6 Step Edge Case Testing
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the question type (Yes/No or Value). Step 2: Test Statement I using extreme values (0, negative numbers, fractions). Step 3: Test Statement II similarly. Step 4: Combine both statements and check all possibilities. Step 5: Verify whether the answer remains the same in every case. Step 6: If only one definite conclusion exists, the data is sufficient.

sections.title: Infinite vs Unique Solution Trap
sections.content: If an equation only provides a relationship but not a definite value, infinite solutions may exist. Example: x + y = 10. If x and y are integers, many pairs are possible. Without an additional condition, the data is insufficient.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Drawing conclusions from only one example. 2. Ignoring zero or negative values. 3. Not checking all cases in absolute value problems. 4. Assuming NO in Yes/No questions means insufficient data.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In Level 3, test each statement using extreme and edge cases. If every possible scenario leads to the same conclusion (YES or NO), the data is sufficient. If even one case produces a different result, the data is insufficient.

tricks.title: Prime Test Shortcut
tricks.explanation: If a number is even and greater than 2, it cannot be prime.
tricks.example: x > 2 and x is even → definite answer NO.

tricks.title: Remainder Trap Check
tricks.explanation: If n leaves remainder 1 when divided by 6, then n = 6k + 1.
tricks.example: k is unknown → n is not fixed.

tricks.title: Absolute Value Three-Case Rule
tricks.explanation: Check three cases: both positive, both negative, and one positive while the other negative.
tricks.example: If inequality changes in any case → insufficient.

tricks.title: Zero Inclusion Rule
tricks.explanation: If it is not stated that x ≠ 0, consider x = 0 as a possible value.
tricks.example: If xy > 0 is not given → x or y could be zero.

tricks.title: Fraction Testing
tricks.explanation: If integer is not specified, fractional values are also possible.
tricks.example: x + y = 2 → x = 1.5 and y = 0.5 is also possible.

tricks.title: Combinatorics Multiple Value Check
tricks.explanation: If nCr = 10, multiple values of n may satisfy the condition.

tricks.title: Probability Integer Check
tricks.explanation: If probability leads to number of objects, check whether only one integer solution exists.

tricks.title: Dependent Equation Identification
tricks.explanation: If both statements together still give the same relationship, infinite solutions exist.

tricks.title: YES/NO Consistency Rule
tricks.explanation: If the answer is NO in every possible case, the data is sufficient.
tricks.example: Inequality is false in all cases → sufficient.

tricks.title: Edge Case Final Check
tricks.explanation: Test positive, negative, and zero values. Only if the result remains the same is the data sufficient.
tricks.example: If one case gives a different result → insufficient.
